title: Prove your care: an honest case, your story, a 90-day habit

say: Prove your care: an honest case, your story, and a 90-day habit.
This is the video for module four of Customer Care and Respectful Communication.
Almost everyone says, I'm good with people. Very few can prove it. In this module you turn your practice into proof, starting with one real customer interaction, written up honestly.

panel.heading: Everyone says they are good with people
items: Tell it as a short, specific story

say: Then you learn to tell it as a short story to an employer, a client or your own customers.

panel.heading: Everyone says they are good with people
items: Tell it as a short, specific story

say: And you build one habit that keeps your care strong after the course ends.

panel.heading: Everyone says they are good with people
items: Tell it as a short, specific story

say: Choose a real complaint, a difficult enquiry or a respectful refusal. A real, imperfect case is worth far more than a perfect story that never happened.

panel.heading: The six-part case template
items: What I did: acknowledge, understand, resolve

say: Describe the situation in two or three sentences, then what the customer needed and how she felt.

panel.heading: The six-part case template
items: What I did: acknowledge, understand, resolve

say: List what you did in order, labelled acknowledge, understand, resolve and follow up.

panel.heading: The six-part case template
items: What I did: acknowledge, understand, resolve

say: Give the outcome with numbers where possible.

panel.heading: The six-part case template
items: What I did: acknowledge, understand, resolve

say: Then say what you would change, and attach evidence such as your notebook entry. Part five matters most, so be specific. I would message earlier is useful. I would do better is not.

panel.heading: The six-part case template
items: What I did: acknowledge, understand, resolve

say: Halima's earlier client overran, and her customer Zainab was angry that nobody warned her. She needed her hair done for an event that evening.
Halima acknowledged: you're right, I should have told you. I'm sorry. Then she asked what time Zainab had to leave.

card.title: A late braiding appointment
card.note: Amount Zainab paid. Prices are approximate.

say: The agreed price was about 12,000 naira.

card.title: A late braiding appointment
card.note: Amount Zainab paid. Prices are approximate.

say: She offered two choices: 1,500 naira off, or a free rebooking the next morning. Zainab chose the discount, and Halima's assistant helped so she finished on time.

card.title: A late braiding appointment
card.note: Amount Zainab paid. Prices are approximate.

say: Zainab paid 10,500 naira and booked again three weeks later.
And what would Halima change? She knew by 9:30 that she would run late. Now she messages any customer as soon as she expects a delay of more than 15 minutes.

say: Before you use a screenshot or comment, ask: may I use your message, with your name and number hidden, as an example of my work? If she says no, describe it in your own words.
Hide names, numbers, addresses and faces. And never change numbers or invent a happy ending. An honest mixed outcome is stronger evidence.

panel.heading: Before you use any evidence
items: Use first names or a customer
Never invent or polish the facts

say: For example, Aisha is applying to be a supermarket cashier. Situation: at the POS stand where I worked, the network went down while 12 customers were waiting.

panel.heading: The STAR story, in about one minute
items: Task: what you had to achieve
Action: what you did, step by step

say: Task: I needed to keep them calm without making promises I couldn't keep.

panel.heading: The STAR story, in about one minute
items: Task: what you had to achieve
Action: what you did, step by step

say: Action: I told everyone straight away, wrote down the queue order, and served the two older customers first after asking the others.

panel.heading: The STAR story, in about one minute
items: Task: what you had to achieve
Action: what you did, step by step

say: Result: 10 of the 12 finished that afternoon, and no one left angry.

panel.heading: The STAR story, in about one minute
items: Task: what you had to achieve
Action: what you did, step by step

say: Keep the set-up short, say I, not we, never blame the customer, and never claim a result you did not achieve. Employers often call referees.

panel.heading: The STAR story, in about one minute
items: Task: what you had to achieve
Action: what you did, step by step
panel.rule: Most of your minute goes on Action and Result

say: For example, Ifeoma bakes cakes in Asaba, and her notebook shows few repeat orders.

panel.heading: When [trigger], I will [action]
items: Tick each time; mark each miss

say: Her habit: when I deliver a cake, I will send a follow-up message within two days. The trigger reminds her, and the action is small enough to do every time. Choose one habit only.

panel.heading: When [trigger], I will [action]
items: Tick each time; mark each miss

say: In week 1 she followed up 11 of 14 deliveries, about 79 percent. By day 30, it was 48 of 52, about 92 percent.

panel.heading: When [trigger], I will [action]
items: Tick each time; mark each miss

say: By the third month, 9 customers reordered, up from 4. She says repeat orders rose while she used the habit, without claiming it was the only cause.

panel.heading: When [trigger], I will [action]
items: Tick each time; mark each miss

say: To remember. Write one real case in six parts. Ask permission and hide personal details. Tell your story with STAR.
Build one small habit and track it. And always be honest about what really happened.

panel.heading: Remember
items: One real case, in six parts
STAR: most time on Action and Result
One habit: when trigger, I will action
Be honest about cause and effect

say: Now write your first case, record your one-minute STAR story, and write your 90-day habit plan with three review dates.
